title: Optane Memory Mode, fixed: associative tag-in-ECC cache over CXL flash
idea: Optane's Memory Mode died on direct-mapped DRAM-cache conflict misses that exposed 300+ ns media. Replace it with a 4-way set-associative near-memory DRAM cache whose tags and way-predictor live in DDR5 ECC spare bits, fronting a cheap CXL SLC-NAND tier, with promotion only on second touch to stop cache pollution.
why: Cost per bit / DRAM scarcity: servers ship ~1/4 the DRAM for big, skewed footprints; conflict misses fall ~3-5x vs direct-mapped, keeping slowdown <10% while 75% of capacity is ~5x cheaper NAND.

title: VMware page sharing, fixed: timing-equalized dedup with uniform write faults
idea: Transparent Page Sharing was disabled by default after Flush+Reload and Dedup-Est-Machina exploited copy-on-write timing. Re-enable cross-VM dedup but force every write to any merge-candidate page through an identical pre-allocated fault path (shared or not) and flush shared lines on cross-domain access, so the timing oracle disappears.
why: Restores the 20-40% DRAM savings TPS gave dense VDI/cloud hosts, cutting DRAM per VM at ~1-2% write-path overhead.

title: IBM MXT, fixed: compression moved behind CXL where latency is free
idea: MXT (2000) compressed all memory in 1 KB sectors behind a 32 MB L3, so every miss paid decompression and the extra cache chip cost more than the DRAM saved. Put an LZ4/zstd engine inside a CXL Type-3 expander that already costs ~150-250 ns, compress at 4 KB with a 64 MB uncompressed hot-line buffer, and expose 2-3x physical capacity as plain memory.
why: Cost per bit: 2-3x effective GB in the far tier; decompression hides inside the existing CXL hop, removing the latency and cost penalty that killed MXT.

title: SoftRAM 95 lesson: audited effective-GB rating for memory compression
idea: Syncronys' SoftRAM 95 sold 'RAM doubling' that did nothing, poisoning trust in memory compression for decades. Create an independent, FTC-backed certification that measures delivered effective GB on standard workload traces, so OEMs can sell and procurement can count 'certified 1.6x effective memory' with smaller physical DRAM.
why: Demand-side supply: if buyers trust 1.5-2x compressed capacity, DRAM content per laptop/phone/server can drop 25-40% during the shortage.

title: Transcendent memory, fixed: rack-pooled ephemeral page cache over CXL switch
idea: Linux cleancache/frontswap were deleted because only Xen used them and copies were synchronous per hypervisor. Rebuild tmem's put/get-may-fail semantics on a CXL 3 switch-attached rack pool with async DMA: hosts push clean page-cache pages to the pool and drop them locally, and the pool may discard anything anytime, so no coherence or durability is needed.
why: Hosts stop overprovisioning page cache; ~20-30% less DRAM per server since clean data is held once per rack and can be dropped safely.

title: HICAMP, fixed: content-addressed dedup hidden inside a CXL memory device
idea: Stanford's HICAMP stored memory as deduplicated immutable 64 B lines linked in DAGs but died because it needed a new CPU and programming model. Implement it inside a CXL expander that presents a flat address space: writes hash each line, a line-ID table maps addresses to unique content, and reference counts free lines, so VM images, checkpoints and string-heavy heaps dedup with zero software change.
why: Dedup ratios of 1.5-4x on VM/container fleets and multi-model serving cut physical DRAM per workload with no ISA change.

title: AMD HBCC, fixed: hardware-paged HBM cache with attention-aware prefetch
idea: Vega's High-Bandwidth Cache Controller paged system memory into VRAM in hardware but died because games fit in VRAM anyway. Revive it for LLM serving: HBM becomes a hardware-managed page cache over host LPDDR/CXL, and the prefetcher uses the previous decode step's attention-score sparsity to fetch only KV pages likely to be attended next.
why: HBM per GPU can drop 2-4x for long-context serving (HBM costs ~3x wafer area per bit); decode access is predictable enough to hide the far-tier latency.

title: x32 ABI, fixed: automatic per-heap 32-bit pointer compression in LLVM
idea: The x32 ABI (32-bit pointers on x86-64) died because every library and distro had to be rebuilt for a new ABI. Instead, an LLVM pass plus allocator places each data structure in a 4 GB 'pointer island' and rewrites interior pointers as 32-bit base-relative offsets (like Java compressed oops / V8 pointer compression), leaving the external ABI untouched.
why: Pointer-heavy workloads (graphs, B-trees, KV stores, compilers) shrink 20-40% in DRAM footprint without an ABI break.

title: Flikker, fixed: auto byte-plane split, MSBs in DRAM, LSBs offloaded
idea: Flikker/EnerJ approximate memory died on programmer annotation burden. The memory controller splits pages tagged as FP tensors by the ML framework's allocator (no annotations) into byte-planes: exponent/high-mantissa planes stay in DRAM, low-mantissa planes go to a CXL flash tier and are fetched only when a kernel requests full precision.
why: Most kernels run on the high planes, so weights/activations/optimizer state need ~50% of the DRAM: ~1.5-2x effective capacity.

title: Micron Automata Processor reborn as CXL-side predicate filter
idea: Micron's in-DRAM NFA Automata Processor died as a standalone PCIe card with proprietary tooling and no killer app. Embed the NFA/predicate fabric inside a CXL memory expander and compile it from standard SQL WHERE clauses and regexes (DuckDB/Postgres plugin), so scans run where cold tables live and only matching rows enter host DRAM.
why: Host DRAM working set for analytics shrinks by the filter selectivity (often 10-100x); cold tables stay on cheaper far memory.

title: Lisp-machine cdr-coding revived as hardware next-pointer elision
idea: Symbolics/LMI cdr-coding replaced next-pointers with 2-bit tags when list cells were contiguous, and died with Lisp machines. Add a memory-side 'implicit successor' bit per 16 B chunk: allocators place linked nodes contiguously, the controller drops the 8 B pointer whenever next == this+size, and reconstructs it on load.
why: Linked lists, trees and graph adjacency structures lose 25-50% of their bytes, shrinking DRAM for pointer-chasing workloads.

title: HP The Machine, minus memristor: rack single-copy read-only data
idea: HP's The Machine died because its memristor never shipped, orphaning a sound idea: fabric-attached memory shared by many nodes. Use CXL 3 shared memory with commodity DRAM to hold exactly one rack-wide copy of read-only data (model weights, reference genomes, dictionaries, container layers) mapped read-only into every host.
why: Eliminates N per-host copies; for a 16-host rack serving the same models, weight DRAM drops ~10x.

title: Sun Rock scout threads, fixed: compiler helper threads hide far memory
idea: Sun's Rock used hardware 'scout' threads to run ahead and prefetch but was cancelled for power and complexity. Do it in software: the compiler emits a stripped address-generation slice that runs on an SMT sibling ahead of the main thread, prefetching from a slow CXL/NAND tier into cache so most data can live off-DRAM.
why: Lets 60-80% of capacity move to a 5-10x cheaper, 3-10x slower tier while hiding most of its latency for irregular code.

title: Fairchild CCD memory, refit as transistor-free KV-cache shift banks
idea: 1970s CCD memories were denser than DRAM but lost on random-access latency. Attention reads every token's K and V in order each decode step, so build KV banks as CCD shift registers (no access transistor per bit, ~2-4F^2) that circulate continuously past a sense row synchronized to the decode loop.
why: Density/cost per bit for the KV cache (often >50% of inference memory): removes per-cell transistors and most row/column periphery.

title: HMC logic layer, fixed: KV vector-quantization codec in HBM base die
idea: Hybrid Memory Cube put logic under DRAM but died with no killer function and proprietary SerDes. Give the HBM4 custom base die one job: a vector-quantization codec that stores KV blocks as per-layer codebook indices plus small residuals and expands them on read, with codebooks held in base-die SRAM.
why: 2-4x more KV per HBM stack without GPU kernel changes, attacking HBM's ~3x area-per-bit tax.

title: Global Memory Service, fixed: a spot market for idle fleet DRAM
idea: UW's 1990s Global Memory Service paged to idle workstations' RAM but died on 10 Mb/s networks and owners' lack of incentive. With 400G RDMA, run an internal spot market where hosts post unused DRAM at a price, borrowers bid for 1 GB revocable leases, and the scheduler packs elastic jobs onto borrowed memory.
why: Clouds strand 25-50% of provisioned DRAM; pricing it unlocks that supply without buying new chips.

title: Diablo Memory1 lesson: royalty-free patent pool for memory tiering
idea: Diablo's Memory1 (flash on a DIMM used as memory) died largely from a Netlist patent suit and single-platform qualification. Form a defensive, royalty-free OIN-style patent pool covering flash/CXL memory tiering, page promotion and DIMM buffering so tiering vendors and hyperscalers can ship without existential lawsuit risk.
why: Removes the legal risk that killed tiered-memory products, accelerating adoption of 2-5x cheaper capacity tiers.

title: AMD HSA, fixed: kill shadow copies with shared virtual memory
idea: AMD's HSA/hUMA promised CPU-GPU shared pointers but died from a weak software ecosystem. Inference stacks today keep a host pinned copy, a framework copy and a GPU copy of weights; enforce single-copy with HSA-style shared page tables where the GPU maps host LPDDR directly and loaders mmap checkpoints instead of reading them into buffers.
why: Removes 2-3 redundant copies of multi-GB models in host DRAM: ~30-60% less host DRAM per inference node.

title: IBM expanded storage, fixed: synchronous page-move to a cheap tier
idea: IBM mainframe Expanded Storage (1985-2000s) was a cheaper DRAM tier reached by a synchronous page-move instruction, retired when 64-bit addressing made it look unnecessary. Revive it as an ISA/CXL instruction that moves a 4 KB page between near DRAM and a compressed or LPDDR far tier in ~1 us with no page fault or I/O stack.
why: Swap-in at ~1 us instead of 10-100 us lets OSes run with 30-50% smaller near DRAM and negligible stalls.

title: Transparent huge pages, fixed: per-4KB valid bitmap stops bloat
idea: Databases disable THP because 2 MB pages physically back untouched memory and bloat RSS. Give each 2 MB TLB entry a 512-bit valid bitmap read by the page-table walker so only touched 4 KB frames are physically backed, keeping TLB reach without the bloat.
why: Recovers the 10-30% of DRAM lost to huge-page bloat on memory-heavy services.

title: Memory ballooning, fixed: controller-tracked zero lines for instant overcommit
idea: Balloon drivers fail in practice: slow, guest-cooperative and prone to thrash. The memory controller tracks all-zero and guest-hinted free lines in a bitmap, returns backing frames to the hypervisor instantly, and materializes zeros on read, so overcommit no longer depends on guest drivers.
why: Enables safe 1.3-1.5x VM overcommit, cutting DRAM per host.

title: Doppelganger cache, fixed: approximate dedup of near-identical KV blocks
idea: The Doppelganger approximate cache (2015) mapped similar-valued blocks to one copy but died because general programs need exact data. LLM KV caches tolerate it: LSH-hash each 16-token KV block and map blocks within cosine >0.995 across requests and layers to one physical block plus a small residual.
why: Shared-context and templated workloads see 1.5-3x KV footprint reduction, and KV dominates inference DRAM/HBM.

title: LLNL ZFP arrays, fixed: lossy compression as a page attribute
idea: ZFP fixed-rate lossy floating-point compression saw low adoption because codes had to be rewritten around compressed-array classes. Put a ZFP engine in the memory controller and let the OS mark pages 'fp64 lossy, 16 bits/value', so unmodified HPC codes get 4x compression with bounded error.
why: ~4x effective DRAM for simulation fields, so HPC nodes need far less DRAM.

title: Z-RAM, fixed: floating-body cells for microsecond-lived activations only
idea: Z-RAM (Innovative Silicon) died because floating-body charge retention was too short and variable for 64 ms DRAM duty. Use capacitorless floating-body cells only for data whose lifetime is microseconds, such as pipelined activations between layers, so the retention spec drops ~1000x and no refresh logic is needed in a ~4F^2 SOI cell.
why: Moves activation buffers out of DRAM/HBM into on-die capacitorless cells ~5x denser than SRAM with zero refresh energy.

title: Bubble memory, fixed: magnetic loop memory for sequentially-read KV
idea: Magnetic bubble memory (TI, Intel Magnetics) died on millisecond serial access through major/minor loops. Attention reads all K/V in order every decode step, so store KV in domain-wall racetrack loops that shift continuously in lockstep with the token loop, re-synced every lap by a marker domain so positioning errors never accumulate.
why: Capacitorless, transistor-sparse, refresh-free KV storage at potentially <4F^2/bit for the largest inference memory consumer.

title: InPhase holography, fixed: optical associative attention over KV keys
idea: InPhase's holographic disc died because tape and disk won archival storage. Use holography where it is unbeatable, parallel correlation: record key vectors as a volume hologram in a photorefractive crystal, shine the query as a beam, read correlation peaks on a camera to get top-k token indices, then fetch only those V vectors from flash.
why: Full keys never sit in DRAM/HBM; million-token attention fetches only top-k values, cutting KV memory >10x.

title: HPE memristor, fixed: stochastic switching as probabilistic optimizer counters
idea: HPE's memristor died because its stochastic, variable switching made it unreliable storage. Turn the flaw into the feature: store Adam moments as Morris-style probabilistic counters in memristor crossbars, where each pulse switches a cell with a known probability, giving unbiased stochastic rounding for free.
why: Optimizer state (8-12 B/param) dominates training memory; ~1 B/param probabilistic counters cut it ~8x with no capacitor and no DRAM.

title: Mythic analog flash CIM, fixed: only cold MoE experts
idea: Mythic's analog flash compute-in-memory went bankrupt in 2022 on ADC overhead, drift and dense models outgrowing the chip. Narrow it to rarely-activated MoE experts: they live as conductances in NOR flash arrays and compute in place, while hot experts and attention stay digital, and the low duty cycle leaves time for drift recalibration.
why: Cold expert weights (often 80%+ of an MoE's bytes) never occupy DRAM/HBM.

title: eASIC structured ASIC, fixed: via-programmed ROM holding frozen weights
idea: Mask ROM died because every code change needed a full mask set, and eASIC's single-via customization never found volume. Store a frozen production model's weights in a via-programmable ROM fabric where one cheap non-EUV via mask encodes the bits, so a model update costs one mask and a two-week spin, not a new chip.
why: Weights at ~1 via per bit with no capacitor, refresh or DRAM; capital and energy per bit fall sharply for long-lived models.

title: Optane App Direct, fixed: read-only weights served from NAND
idea: Optane persistent memory died partly on crash-consistency programming complexity and write wear. Sidestep both by exposing only immutable data: a CXL controller maps SLC NAND as read-only load/store memory, caches 256 B sectors in the NAND dies' own page-buffer latches, and serves model weights and embedding tables with no DRAM buffer.
why: Read-mostly data moves to ~10x cheaper-per-bit NAND, and no persistence-semantics or endurance problem remains.

title: Cell SPE local stores, fixed: compiler-scheduled flash-to-SRAM layer streaming
idea: Cell's SPEs died because programmers hand-wrote double-buffered DMA into 256 KB local stores. Transformer inference is a fully static dataflow, so the compiler generates the DMA schedule: stream layer N+1 weights from NVMe flash into SRAM while layer N computes, picking batch size so compute time covers flash read time.
why: DRAM-free throughput inference servers with only SRAM and flash, removing multi-GB DRAM per accelerator.

title: Tera MTA, fixed: barrel-threaded cores running graphs from flash
idea: Tera/Cray XMT hid memory latency with 128 hardware threads per core but lost on single-thread performance. Put XMT-style barrel cores (thousands of threads, SRAM register files) inside an SSD controller so graph analytics run directly against NAND's ~20 us reads, with throughput coming from concurrency instead of DRAM.
why: Trillion-edge graphs run without TB-scale DRAM on ~10-20x cheaper-per-bit NAND.

title: Approximate MLC storage, fixed: precision-tiered flash cells for KV
idea: Sampson et al.'s approximate MLC storage never shipped because general files cannot tolerate errors. KV caches can: write sign/exponent/high-mantissa bits to SLC-mode pages and low-mantissa bits to QLC-mode pages with relaxed program-verify, raising density and cutting program time for the error-tolerant bits.
why: Offloaded KV in flash at ~2x density with faster writes, so no DRAM is needed for cold KV beyond a small working window.

title: T-RAM, fixed: replica-tracked thyristor bias for on-die KV window
idea: T-RAM Semiconductor died because thyristor holding current shifts strongly with temperature, ruining margins. Add a per-bank replica thyristor and closed-loop bias generator that tracks temperature and process in real time, and use the dense capacitorless array as an on-die 'hot KV window' for the most recent few thousand tokens.
why: Thyristor cells ~2x denser than SRAM on logic keep hot KV on-die, so less HBM/DRAM is required.

title: Nantero NRAM, fixed: BEOL-only CNT fab hybrid-bonded to logic
idea: Nantero's carbon-nanotube NRAM stalled because fabs feared CNT contamination of front-end lines and integration took a decade. Fabricate the CNT switching layer in a dedicated BEOL-only fab on wafers carrying only select transistors, then hybrid-bond them to logic, so no mainline fab ever touches nanotubes.
why: A nonvolatile, refresh-free, capacitorless tier replacing part of DRAM, buildable in small, cheap U.S. BEOL fabs.

title: Reversible computing, fixed: integer-exact reversible layers erase activation storage
idea: RevNets and reversible computing were abandoned because floating-point inversion drifts and reconstruction errors accumulate. Build transformer blocks from fixed-point additive couplings computed in modular integer arithmetic (y = x + f(x) mod 2^k), which are bit-exactly invertible, so backprop recomputes every activation from the output and stores none.
why: Training activation memory (often 50%+ of training memory) becomes O(1) in depth, with no storage of any kind.

title: Value prediction, fixed: store only predictor residuals off critical path
idea: Load-value prediction never entered CPUs because mispredictions cost pipeline flushes. Reuse stride, context and small learned predictors as a memory codec: on write store only the residual from the prediction in SRAM or flash, on read run the predictor and add the residual, so a misprediction costs only extra bits.
why: Smooth data (sensor streams, counters, indices, embeddings) compresses 2-5x, letting SRAM/flash-only devices hold working sets that used to need DRAM.

title: Graphcore IPU, fixed: hybrid-bonded MRAM weight die under SRAM
idea: Graphcore's SRAM-only IPU faded because 900 MB on-chip could not hold modern models and its DDR streaming was slow. Hybrid-bond a read-optimized STT-MRAM die (weights are written rarely, so slow high-energy writes and limited endurance do not matter) directly under the compute die at >10 TB/s.
why: Gigabytes of weights per package with no DRAM or HBM; MRAM is capacitorless, nonvolatile and ~3-4x denser than SRAM.

title: Poly-load 4T SRAM, fixed: BEOL oxide-TFT loads atop logic
idea: 1990s 4T SRAM with polysilicon resistor loads was dropped for standby current and poor stability. Replace the resistors with ultra-low-leakage oxide-semiconductor TFT pull-ups stacked in the BEOL directly above the four silicon transistors, so the cell's silicon footprint is ~60% of 6T while static stability returns.
why: ~1.6x denser capacitorless SRAM on logic, enabling bigger on-die buffers that replace DRAM in edge and AI chips.

title: Feature-phone NOR XIP, fixed: profile-clustered execute-in-place, DRAM-less SoCs
idea: Execute-in-place from NOR flash ran feature phones with little DRAM but was abandoned as code bloated and random fetches stalled. Profile-guided linking clusters hot code and read-only data into contiguous flash pages fronted by a 32-64 MB on-die SRAM cache, so edge AI devices, IoT and controllers ship with zero DRAM.
why: Removes DRAM entirely from billions of low-end devices, freeing supply for servers.

title: Everspin MRAM, fixed: MRAM write-combining journal makes NAND workable memory
idea: Everspin MRAM never reached Gb density, so it never replaced DRAM. Use a small MRAM as a nonvolatile write-combining journal in front of NAND: random 64 B stores land in MRAM at ns latency, are coalesced into full NAND pages in the background, and reads check the MRAM index first.
why: Lets NAND serve as main memory for write-active data, not just read-only data, with no DRAM buffer and no capacitor-backed power-loss protection.

title: IBM TrueNorth, fixed: delta-event storage of token activations
idea: TrueNorth's event-driven spiking design faded because spiking nets could not be trained to state of the art. Keep its useful trick of storing only changes: hidden states across adjacent tokens or frames are kept in SRAM as sparse thresholded deltas against the previous step, with periodic keyframes like a video codec.
why: Streaming inference (video, audio, agents) cuts activation/KV memory 3-10x where inputs change slowly.

title: Connection Machine, fixed: bit-serial compute inside cache SRAM arrays
idea: Thinking Machines' CM-1 used 65,536 bit-serial processors with private memory and died on cost and programmability. Do bit-serial compute inside existing SRAM subarrays by activating two wordlines and sensing bitline AND/NOR on transposed data, so each bitline is a processor and activations are processed where they sit.
why: Activations never leave SRAM, so DRAM staging buffers between layers disappear for small and mid-size models.

title: Optane latency, fixed: look-ahead MoE router hides flash fetch
idea: Optane failed partly because software could not hide its latency on unpredictable accesses. Co-design the model instead: train each MoE router to choose experts for layer L+2 from layer L's hidden state, giving two layers of warning to fetch expert weights from flash into SRAM before they are needed.
why: MoE models with hundreds of GB of experts serve from flash plus SRAM, driving weight DRAM toward zero.

title: ZFS dedup's RAM hunger, fixed: flash-resident delta store for fine-tunes
idea: ZFS dedup became notorious for needing ~5 GB of RAM per TB for its dedup table. Serve thousands of fine-tuned model variants by content-defined chunking of weight tensors into flash, with an SRAM cuckoo filter (~1 byte per chunk) to spot duplicate chunks and a flash-resident index, so each variant costs only its unique delta.
why: Multi-tenant fine-tune serving without N copies in DRAM: 10-100x fewer bytes for near-identical variants.

title: EIE sparse engine, fixed: fixed-rate tANS weights decoded at MACs
idea: EIE/Deep Compression's Huffman-coded sparse weights never took off because variable-length decode stalled lockstep hardware. Use block-fixed-rate tANS: each 256-weight block is coded to an exact bit budget with per-block tables, so parallel decoders at every MAC column run in lockstep straight from compressed SRAM.
why: Weights held at ~2.5-3 bits on SRAM-only chips: ~1.5-2x more model per mm^2 with no DRAM.
